vignette:
Mr. Ahmed sits at his pottery wheel in the small shed behind his house, his hands buried in wet clay. The wheel spins, but his fingers hesitate. For a moment, the cool, smooth earth under his palms is not clay but something else—mud, thick and red, clinging to his clothes as he stumbled through a flooded paddy field. He blinks, and the image dissolves. His wife, Maya, calls from the kitchen that tea is ready. He does not answer. He cannot. The sound of her voice, so familiar, sometimes sharpens into a different voice—his mother’s, screaming his name as the flames rose over the village.

He was twenty-seven then, living in a small town in what is now Bangladesh. The year was 1971. War had come to his doorstep. One night, soldiers arrived. He remembers the smell of burning jute and the shouts in a language he did not want to understand. He grabbed his wife and his youngest daughter, who was three at the time, and they ran. They ran through the dark, through the mud, through a river that tasted of copper and smoke. They hid in a bamboo grove for three days without food, listening to the distant thud of mortars. His daughter cried, and he covered her mouth with his hand, praying she would not choke on her own sobs. She stopped crying on the second day. On the third day, she was still. He never forgave himself for that silence.

They crossed the border into India as refugees. He found shelter in a camp, then a small room in Calcutta. He had no kiln, no wheel, no clay. He had been a potter since childhood—his father had taught him on the banks of the Padma River. In exile, his hands ached for the wet earth. He took work hauling bricks, and at night he would press his fingers into the dust, trying to remember the shape of a pot. The memory of his daughter, the one he could not save, was a shard lodged in his chest. He never spoke of her to anyone, not even to Maya. The other children who survived—two sons born later in India—grew up knowing only that their father was quiet, that he worked with clay, and that he sometimes woke up shouting in the dark.

Forty years later, he lives in a quiet suburb of Toronto, in a house with a small garden. His sons are engineers, married with children. Maya still makes tea with cardamom. His pottery business is modest—he sells bowls and vases at a local market, and his hands, though stiff with arthritis, still remember the old rhythms. But the wheel is no longer a comfort. He avoids certain clays because their color reminds him of the river at dusk. The sound of a helicopter passing overhead makes him drop a pot before it reaches the wheel. He has not visited a park with open fields since the war, and he refuses to attend any large family gathering that might echo the noise of a crowd.

Some nights, he lies awake, his heart pounding over nothing. He checks the locks on the doors three times before bed. He has not wept in decades, but he cannot stop thinking about the mud, the bamboo, the small hand that went limp in his. His PCL-5 score of 50 reflects the weight he carries: the intrusive images that surface when he sees a child’s shoe at the market, the startle response when a car backfires, the persistent guilt that he chose to live when others did not. He still sits at the wheel every morning, but lately he has been making only small clay figures—tiny, faceless bodies that he fires in the kiln and then crushes into dust before Maya can see them.
